conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for making time for this. I’m Dr. Ramirez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is to listen and help figure out how you’re really doing now that your baby is here.

To do that, I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply ten questions about how you’ve felt over the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting—just a snapshot of your emotional well-being so we can make sure you get the support you deserve.

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger. We’ll go at your pace, and you can pause or skip anything that feels uncomfortable. Ready to jump in?

1. In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

(Hesitates, then gives a small shrug)  
Sometimes… like, every now and then I’ll catch myself smiling at something silly the baby does, but it feels kind of forced. Mostly I just feel too tired and down to really laugh—nothing feels that funny anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I mean, I try when my partner jokes around, but it feels flat, like I’m just pretending. Most of the time I’m too worn-out or sad to find things funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much… I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels kind of “why bother.” I still go through the motions, hoping I’ll feel something, but the spark just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty often. If the baby fusses for a long time, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not comforting him right or I missed some cue. Even little stuff, like forgetting to switch the laundry, turns into “I’m failing at everything.” I know it’s not totally logical, but the guilt just pops up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes… most days. My mind keeps running through scary “what-ifs” about the baby—what if he stops breathing, what if I drop him, what if there’s something wrong the doctor missed. There’s no real reason, but I can’t shut the thoughts off. Sometimes I can talk myself down, but they come right back the next time he stirs.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week… Out of nowhere my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t get a full breath, like something awful is about to happen even when everything looks fine. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and on-edge the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… a lot of the time. Feeding, changing, trying to sleep, keeping the house from falling apart—it all piles up and I feel like I’m drowning. I manage to get through it, but it’s like I’m barely treading water and waiting for the next wave to hit.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t settle. I keep replaying everything I think I did wrong that day, worrying about the baby, worrying I’ll never feel like myself again. It takes me over an hour to drift off, and then I wake up a couple times with my heart pounding. Even when the baby’s quiet, I can’t stay asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most days… It’s like a gray cloud that just hangs there. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel tears in my throat for no clear reason. I keep telling myself I should be happy—he’s healthy, I’m lucky—but the sadness feels heavier than anything else right now.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times this week. Once was after a long night when he wouldn’t settle—I just sat on the couch holding him and crying quietly so I wouldn’t wake anyone. Another time was when my mom asked how I was doing; the question itself made me tear up and I couldn’t stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…a couple of fleeting thoughts have popped up, like “what if I just wasn’t here,” but I’ve never planned anything and I don’t want to die. They scare me when they show up, and I push them away because I know I need to be here for my baby.

You've shared that over the past week most days feel heavy and gray: laughter rarely comes, activities you once anticipated now feel pointless, and you often blame yourself when anything goes wrong. <sym>Anxiety</sym> about the baby's safety races through your mind most of the day, and sudden <sym>panic sensations</sym> leave you shaky. You feel overwhelmed, <sym>can't sleep</sym> even when the baby is quiet, cry easily, and have fleeting thoughts of <sym>not wanting to be here</sym>-though you quickly push them away because you want to care for your child.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>"Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself 'pretty often' and gives multiple examples of pervasive self-blame, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent, intrusive worries occurring "most days" with racing thoughts and inability to control them, aligning with "Yes, very often."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense episodes of panic with physical and cognitive symptoms occurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed most of the time, barely coping and anticipating the next wave of stress, aligning with inability to cope at all.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to racing anxious thoughts, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "most days" with persistent tearfulness, clear match for "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes crying episodes twice this week, clearly triggered by feeling overwhelmed and emotionally raw, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26/30 places well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major depression. The patient endorses <sym>depressed mood most days</sym>, <sym>marked loss of interest</sym>, <sym>self-reproach</sym>, <sym>recurrent anxiety</sym>, <sym>panic attacks</sym>, <sym>feelings of inadequacy</sym>, and <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, together meeting core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Item 10 ≥1 mandates immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>obstetrician, PCP, or perinatal psychiatrist</med>
2. Develop a written safety plan and provide 24-h crisis hotline numbers
3. Initiate weekly evidence-based therapy such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med>
4. Discuss risks/benefits of starting an <med>SSRI compatible with breastfeeding</med>
5. Involve partner/family in monitoring mood and caring for baby to reduce overload
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to track symptom change
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Screening Summary – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-based self-report with elaborative comments.

Symptoms/Concerns endorsed:
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia (loss of interest/pleasure)
- Excessive self-blame and guilt (“failing at everything”)
- Unwarranted anxiety and intrusive “what-ifs” regarding infant safety
- Episodic panic symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness) without clear trigger
- Feeling overwhelmed/drowning in daily tasks
- Initial insomnia and middle-night wakening linked to rumination
- Passive, fleeting self-harm ideation without intent or plan

Patterns:
Symptoms present “most days,” interfere with sleep and enjoyment, and are not limited to transient “baby blues.” Patient remains motivated to care for infant and has protective factors (partner, mother), yet distress is clinically significant.

Risk flags:
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood/anxiety
- High self-criticism and guilt
- Panic-level episodes
- Any mention of self-harm (even passive) → safety issue requiring further evaluation

Screening observation:
Findings suggest probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety, emerging in postpartum period; passive SI noted. Recommend immediate comprehensive mental-health assessment (EPDS score, clinical interview, safety plan) and consideration of therapy/medical management resources.
